## Water Column {#am_wc}

Water column parameters vary in physicochemical stability which, in
turn, affects sample reliability. Temperature, pH and dissolved oxygen
generally must be measured in the field within 15 minutes of sample
collection. Conductivity, salinity, and turbidity may be measured in the
field or sent to a lab for processing which allows for comparable field
and laboratory results to be combined for analysis. The accuracy of
field-probe measurements of chlorophyll a, total suspended solids,
nitrogen and phosphorus is considered lower than laboratory measurements
and often not directly comparable; therefore, only laboratory data were
used in analyses of these parameters.

Nutrients were analyzed from records of total nitrogen and total
phosphorus. If total nitrogen was not measured directly but instead
component nitrogen species such as total Kjeldahl nitrogen, nitrate,
nitrite and ammonia were sampled, total nitrogen was calculated as the
sum of the components.

Water quality was assessed using monthly averages of the following
parameters: water temperature (°C), salinity (ppt), dissolved oxygen
(mg/L), dissolved oxygen saturation (%), and pH (pH units). Water
clarity was analyzed using monthly averages of chlorophyll a (µg/L),
Secchi depth (m), total suspended solids (mg/L), turbidity (NTU), and
colored dissolved organic matter (PCU).

Water column parameters are strongly influenced by the season or month
when samples are collected. For example, nutrient concentrations and
water quality and clarity levels change from the dry season to the rainy
season. Seasonal Kendall tests were applied, where appropriate, to
account for systematic differences in indicator values between months. A
significant result for the Seasonal Kendall test indicates a
monotonically increasing or decreasing trend across seasons or months.
The trend slope estimate is called the Sen slope, or the Theil-Sen
estimator, and is calculated as the median of the slopes between all
pairs of points within each season. The Sen intercept was calculated as
the median of `y – mx` for all year-indicator value pairs in the time
series, where `y` is the indicator value, `m` is the Sen slope, and `x`
is the year corresponding with indicator value `y`.

**Seasonal Kendall-Tau Analysis**

Indicators must have a minimum of five to ten years, depending on the
habitat, of data within the geographic range of the analysis to be
included in the analysis. Ten years of data are required for discrete
parameters, and five years of data are required for continuous
parameters. If there are insufficient years of data, the number of years
of data available will be noted and labeled as "insufficient data to
conduct analysis". Further, for the preferred Seasonal Kendall-Tau test,
there must be data from at least two months in common across at least
two consecutive years within the RCP managed area being analyzed. Values
that pass both of these tests will be included in the analysis and be
labeled as Use_In_Analysis = TRUE. Any that fail either test will be
excluded from the analyses and labeled as Use_In_Analysis = FALSE. The
points for all Water Column plots displayed in this section are monthly
averages. Trend significance will be denoted as "Significant Trend"
(when p \< 0.05), or "Non-significant Trend" (when p \>= 0.05). Any
parameters with insufficient data to perform Seasonal Kendall-Tau test
will have their monthly averages plotted without a corresponding trend
line.

### Nekton {#am_nekton}

Nekton survey data were corrected by sampling effort and
aggregated to plot species richness over time. The effort-corrected
values reflected the gear type and its size, as well as the duration of
the survey tows. The number of unique species encountered by the
comparable group of surveys (i.e., using the same gear type and size)
was summed and then divided by the effort-corrected value to estimate
species richness per 100 m^2^.
